opus-5.5.text:
I think the key thing is that "generalist" and "best at what you actually need" aren't the same. The big frontier models are remarkable, and I spent a lot of my career working on exactly that kind of large-scale pretraining, so I have a lot of respect for them. But they're optimized to be pretty good at everything: writing code, answering trivia, chatting, summarizing. When you care deeply about one class of problems, that breadth comes with real costs.

For us, the first advantage is data. A specialist model lets you be very deliberate about what goes into training. You can curate the modalities that matter, whether that's images, video, audio, or structured signals, and how they line up with each other. A lot of the hard multimodal problems come down to alignment between modalities, and generalist models usually treat that as one objective among many. When it's *the* objective, you can go much deeper.

The second is efficiency. If you're not trying to cover every possible task, you can get frontier-level or better performance on your domain with a much smaller model. That changes the economics completely. Inference is cheaper, latency is lower, and you can deploy in places a giant general model just doesn't fit, like on a device, in a customer's own environment, or in real-time settings.

The third is the feedback loop. When you own the model end to end for a specific use case, every customer interaction tells you something about where the model is failing. You can retrain, fine-tune, and ship improvements quickly. You aren't waiting for a general provider's next release and hoping your problem happened to get better.

And I'd add one more thing: reliability. In a lot of real applications, people don't need a model that can do a thousand things impressively. They need one that does a few things correctly, consistently, every time. Specialization makes that much easier to achieve and to measure.

So it isn't that generalist models are bad. They set an incredible baseline. But the history of this field suggests that once you know exactly what you're solving for, focused data, focused architecture, and focused evaluation tend to win. That's the bet we're making.

r001.rationale: The response says specialist models can deliberately curate the relevant modalities and their alignment, while generalists treat multimodal alignment as one objective among many.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts broad generalist tasks with focused multimodal work, but does not state that general factual knowledge contributes little to multimodal capability.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that generalist models are optimized for breadth, and the problems we care about are defined by depth.

When you build a frontier generalist, every design decision is a compromise across thousands of use cases. The tokenizer, the data mixture, the training objective, the way images or video get compressed into the model's context. All of that is tuned so the model is pretty good at everything. That's genuinely impressive, but "pretty good at everything" is not what a radiologist, or a satellite imagery analyst, or a manufacturing QA team actually needs. They need the model to be excellent at one hard thing, and they need it to fail in predictable ways.

So a specialist model lets us make choices a generalist can't afford. We can spend our compute on much higher-resolution visual inputs instead of downsampling to save tokens. We can curate domain data that a general web crawl simply doesn't contain, or contains in a noisy, mislabeled form. We can design evaluations with actual domain experts and train against the failure modes that matter in that field, rather than against a broad benchmark leaderboard.

There's also a practical business angle. Specialist models are smaller, so inference is cheaper and we can deploy on-prem or at the edge, which is a hard requirement in a lot of regulated or latency-sensitive settings. And because the scope is narrow, we can give customers much stronger guarantees about behavior, data handling, and what happens when the model is uncertain. That's very hard to promise when the same weights are also writing poetry and debugging Python.

I'd add one honest caveat. Generalists are improving fast, and for a lot of mainstream multimodal tasks they'll be good enough. Our bet isn't that specialists win everywhere. It's that in domains where the cost of a wrong answer is high and the data looks nothing like the public internet, a focused model built with people who actually do that work will stay ahead. And when the generalists catch up on a given task, we'll have moved to the next hard problem in the domain, because that's where our customers are already pulling us.

astra-6.text:
I think the advantage comes from focusing on a specific problem and doing it really well. A generalist model has to cover a huge range of tasks. With a specialist multimodal model, we can focus the training, the data, and the evaluation on the kinds of inputs our customers actually work with.

And the value of multimodality is in connecting signals. What you see, what you hear, and what’s written can each tell you something different. The challenge is understanding them together, especially when one signal is ambiguous.

But specialization alone isn’t a moat. We still have to demonstrate that it delivers better accuracy, lower latency, or lower cost on the customer’s task. That’s where I think we can build an advantage: a tighter feedback loop between the problem we’re solving and how we improve the model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the advantage comes from focus. A generalist model has to do a lot of things well. A specialist multimodal model lets us concentrate on how different kinds of information—text, images, audio, and video—work together in a particular task.

Take video: recognizing what’s in an individual frame is only part of the problem. You also need to understand what changes over time, connect that with what’s being said, and identify which moments matter to the user. We can design the training and evaluation around those requirements.

That gives us an opportunity to deliver better quality, lower latency, and lower cost for the use cases we care about. It doesn’t mean a specialist automatically wins. We have to demonstrate that advantage on real customer tasks, and keep improving as generalist models get better.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the advantage to task focus and tailored training and evaluation, but does not say specialist models use a greater concentration of multimodal training data.
